kp.k: Responsible AI development combines infrastructure with service pilots
kp.d: The Legal Design Lab describes an R&D agenda investigating how AI models and agents might empower people facing legal problems and improve providers’ accessibility and equity. Its activities combine user research, system evaluation, community design, shared infrastructure and tool development; the benefits are framed as goals and possibilities rather than demonstrated justice outcomes.
qs: Our team is exploring how AI models and agents might improve the justice system.

The Legal Design Lab is working both on the infrastructure of responsible AI (gathering data, creating labeled datasets, establishing taxonomies, creating benchmarks, and finding pilot partners) as well as the design & development of new AI tech/service pilots.

kp.k: Shared infrastructure aims to reduce duplicated development
kp.d: The Legal Help Commons is presented as shared implementation infrastructure for legal aid organizations, courts and technology partners. Working groups produce reusable resources addressing document extraction, AI-ready knowledge bases and voice intake. The hub describes these resources as enabling adoption of proven workflows rather than rebuilding independently, without supplying comparative implementation results.
qs: The Legal Help Commons is shared infrastructure for AI in the access to justice sector — built so that legal aid organizations, courts, and technology partners can adopt proven AI workflows instead of building from scratch.

It brings together reference architectures, implementation playbooks, evaluation rubrics, and reusable tools around the specific technical challenges the field faces: extracting data from legal documents, building AI-ready knowledge bases, designing voice-based intake systems, and more.
Each group produces playbooks, tested code, and shared standards that any organization can use.

kp.k: JusticeBench maps projects, tasks and evaluation resources
kp.d: JusticeBench is described as a discovery and research platform organizing justice technology projects through a formal task taxonomy and providing benchmarks, datasets and guidance. Its role is distinct from the Commons’ implementation support: it helps funders, researchers and practitioners identify projects and resources rather than itself constituting evidence that those projects improve outcomes.
qs: JusticeBench is a discovery and research platform that maps the landscape of AI and technology projects in the access to justice space.

It catalogs who’s building what, organizes projects by a formal task taxonomy, and provides benchmarks, datasets, and orientation resources for anyone trying to understand what’s happening in justice AI — whether you’re a funder scoping the field, a researcher looking for evaluation data, or a practitioner figuring out where to start.

kp.k: Justice co-pilots target legal aid professional augmentation
kp.d: The Justice AI Co-Pilot project involves scoping, prototyping and piloting tools with legal aid and court groups. Its stated purpose is to help professionals serve more people, especially in eviction defense, housing conditions, reentry and debt relief involving legal financial obligations after criminal justice involvement. This is a professional-support development agenda, not a claim of autonomous lawyer replacement.
qs: The Legal Design Lab is working with legal aid and court groups around the country to scope, prototype, and pilot new AI tools to help legal professionals better serve more of the public.
One focus is on tools for Housing Law — particularly legal groups helping people with eviction defense, living condition problems, and other landlord-tenant issues.

We are also working on Reentry services and Debt Relief, to help providers assist people with legal financial obligations and debts they are struggling with after going through the criminal justice system.

kp.k: Legal answer evaluation incorporates expert reasoning and user needs
kp.d: The Lab describes developing practical legal Q&A criteria through interviews with justice professionals and a rating game combining real questions from prior user interviews with different models’ answers. Professionals explain their ratings aloud, generating labeled judgments and refining the criteria. Automated evaluation is being explored conditionally, with safety explicitly part of the inquiry.
qs: Our Lab (including with our amazing students in Winter Quarter’s AI for Legal Help class) has been establishing a common set of practical, measurable criteria by which we can evaluate AI Legal Q&A.
Having justice professionals play this rating game, and narrate aloud why they are rating the Q-and-A pairs as they do.
Exploring which of the criteria might be evaluated automatically, and exactly how we could safely automate the evaluation.

kp.k: Quality standards research remains explicitly developmental
kp.d: The hub’s abstract for Hagan’s 2023 study proposes 22 criteria for assessing civil justice answers and reports expert review of those criteria. The December 01, 2024 paper describes a multi-stakeholder, mixed-methods, 3-study sequence culminating in a draft evaluation protocol. These are contributions to evaluating usefulness and consumer harms, not reported model performance scores.
qs: This study presents a proposed set of 22 specific criteria to evaluate the quality of a system’s answers to a person’s request for legal help for a civil justice problem.
It also presents the review of these evaluation criteria by legal domain experts like legal aid lawyers, courthouse self help center staff, and legal help website administrators.
It presents the results of a 3-study sequence to identify which specific quality criteria matter most for helping a user seeking legal help, and concludes with a draft quality evaluation protocol.

kp.k: Public research tests trust through fictional legal problems
kp.d: Online and in-court interviews with adults across America examine anticipated and experienced helpfulness and trustworthiness while participants attempt fictional legal problems. Research also investigates harmful responses, desired warnings and ideal interfaces. The February 2024 paper’s summary argues that direct community evidence should counterbalance expert assertions about public needs; the hub provides no interview sample size or quantitative trust findings.
qs: With our online and in-court interviews, we ask people — if they had a fictional legal problem — if they would use AI to address it, and if they do, we watch over their shoulder as they try to use it to address this fictional legal problem.
what people identify as making an AI’s responses helpful, what makes it harmful, and how much warning or disclosures they want

These empirical findings provide directions that can counterbalance legal domain experts’ proposals about the public interest around AI, as expressed by attorneys, court officials, advocates, and regulators.

kp.k: Learned Hands supplies labeled legal issue training data
kp.d: Developed with Suffolk LIT Lab, Learned Hands uses an online game to label people’s stories with standardized legal issue codes. The resulting dataset is intended to support classifiers and other tools that identify legal problems and connect people to help. This describes a data-production mechanism and possible downstream applications, not measured classification performance.
qs: Playing the Learned Hands game lets you label people’s stories with a standardized list of legal issue codes.
The game produces a labeled dataset of people’s stories, tagged with the legal issues that apply to their situation.
This dataset can be used to develop AI tools like classifiers to automatically spot people’s issues.

kp.k: Incident collection tracks harms beyond fabricated legal authorities
kp.d: The planned AI/legal-help incident database solicits specific problematic responses, including incorrect jurisdictional or rights information, fabricated authorities and organizations, irrelevant advice, legal misrepresentation and lost nuance. The page describes collection and review before future release; it does not report incident counts, prevalence or measured hallucination rates.
qs: We will be making this database available in the near-future, as we collect more records & review them.
incorrect information about legal rights, rules, jurisdiction, forms, or organizations;
hallucinations of cases, statutes, organizations, hotlines, or other important legal information;
overly simplified information, that loses key nuance or cautions;

kp.k: Interdisciplinary training centers on real legal aid workflows
kp.d: The 2026 AI for Legal Help course brings law, computer science and policy students into teams partnered directly with attorneys or paralegals. Over nine weeks they map workflows, identify plausible applications and build functional prototypes tested against real cases and feedback. The training incorporates both generative and rules-based AI rather than assuming generative models suit every task.
qs: focused on transforming high-stakes, repeatable legal aid workflows with responsible use of technology — including both generative and rules-based AI solutions.
In this studio course, students from law, computer science, and policy work in interdisciplinary teams to design, build, and evaluate AI-powered tools for legal aid organizations.

Over nine weeks, each team partners directly with a practicing legal aid attorney or paralegal, maps their workflow, identifies where AI could plausibly help, and builds a working prototype — not a mockup or a slide deck, but a functional tool tested against real cases and real feedback.

kp.k: 2026 prototypes span intake, drafting and procedural assistance
kp.d: Winter 2026 involved five teams and three partner organizations: Legal Aid Society of San Bernardino, Legal Aid Society of San Diego and Legal Aid Services of Oklahoma. Projects covered voice intake, attorney-reviewed accommodation letters, self-help motions to set aside, eviction notice defect detection and form preparation, and rules-based expungement screening for junior attorneys. The hub claims the intake system reduces 45-minute manual intake queues but gives no measurement method or reduction magnitude.
qs: In Winter 2026, five teams worked with three partner organizations — Legal Aid Society of San Bernardino, Legal Aid Society of San Diego, and Legal Aid Services of Oklahoma — on challenges spanning housing, eviction defense, and criminal reentry.
a voice AI intake system that screens callers in crisis and reduces 45-minute manual intake queues,
a chatbot that interviews tenants and drafts reasonable accommodation demand letters for attorneys to review,
a rules-based expungement eligibility screener that helps junior attorneys in Oklahoma navigate a notoriously complex statutory landscape.

kp.k: Prototype deployment depends on evaluation and organizational change
kp.d: The 2026 prototypes are being assessed using team-designed rubrics covering accuracy, safety, privacy and human oversight. Spring work is described as further refinement and testing for a possible pilot, including expert and user feedback and potential process and policy changes. The described maturity is therefore prototype development and evaluation, not established scaled deployment.
qs: Each prototype is being evaluated against rubrics the teams themselves designed — for legal accuracy, safety, privacy, and human oversight — and presented to an audience of legal aid directors, court administrators, and justice technology practitioners from across the country.
In Spring Quarter, student teams will continue work on refining, testing, and prepping these prototypes for a possible pilot.
This will involve expert and user feedback sessions, considerations of changing underlying processes and policies, and thinking through responsible and safe deployment challenges.

kp.k: Coordinated governance is proposed to close the justice gap
kp.d: The hub presents ecosystem coordination as necessary to responsible access-to-justice innovation. Its 2024 summit sought a national roadmap for accountable deployment, while a Margaret Hagan post excerpt advocates statewide stewardship beyond speculation and pilots. The second summit, November 20-21, 2025, reportedly convened over 150 participants; attendance documents coordination activity, not demonstrated reductions in unmet legal need.
qs: The Summit’s primary goal was to build strong relationships and a national, coordinated roadmap of how AI can responsibly be deployed and held accountable to close the justice gap.
If AI is going to advance access to justice rather than deepen the justice gap, the public-interest legal field needs more than speculation and pilots — we need statewide stewardship.
The Stanford Legal Design Lab hosted the second annual AI and Access to Justice Summit on November 20-21, 2025.

Over 150 legal professionals, technologists, regulators, strategists, and funders came together to tackle one big question: how can we build a strong, sustainable national/international AI and Access to Justice Ecosystem?

kp.k: LegalBench measures reasoning rather than service delivery outcomes
kp.d: The included LegalBench abstract describes an interdisciplinary academic benchmark containing 162 tasks across six types of legal reasoning and an empirical evaluation of 20 open-source and commercial LLMs. Legal professionals designed tasks to reflect practically useful or interesting reasoning capabilities. The hub reproduces this scope but does not provide model scores or establish effects on legal service outcomes.
qs: we present LegalBench: a collaboratively constructed legal reasoning benchmark consisting of 162 tasks covering six different types of legal reasoning.
LegalBench was built through an interdisciplinary process, in which we collected tasks designed and hand-crafted by legal professionals.
This paper describes LegalBench, presents an empirical evaluation of 20 open-source and commercial LLMs, and illustrates the types of research explorations LegalBench enables.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Stanford Legal Design Lab presents AI as a potential means of expanding public-interest legal services, primarily through professional augmentation and targeted self-help rather than a prediction of lawyer replacement.
pts.d: The Lab says it is developing co-pilots with legal aid and court partners so professionals can serve more people, particularly in eviction defense, housing conditions, reentry and debt relief. The broader claim that AI can make justice more accessible and equitable is framed as an R&D objective and possibility, not a demonstrated sector-wide outcome. Its 2026 course description identifies concrete prototypes: voice intake, tenant interviewing and demand-letter drafting, motion-to-set-aside guidance for unrepresented tenants, eviction-notice defect spotting and court-form pre-population, and rules-based expungement screening. The demand-letter workflow explicitly retains attorney review. The intake description asserts a reduction in 45-minute manual intake queues but supplies no measured reduction or comparison.

pts.k: The Lab claims shared infrastructure can let legal-help organizations reuse AI workflows, while Margaret Hagan argues that statewide stewardship is needed for AI to advance access to justice.
pts.d: The Legal Help Commons is presented as a way to avoid duplicative development through reference architectures, playbooks, evaluation rubrics, tested code and shared standards. JusticeBench is a complementary discovery platform, not a reported model-performance result: it catalogs projects and provides task taxonomies, datasets and benchmarks. Learned Hands produces labeled legal-issue data that the Lab says can support classifiers for automatically identifying people's legal issues and connecting them to help. Separately, the excerpt attributed to Margaret Hagan makes the normative, conditional claim that pilots alone are insufficient and statewide stewardship is necessary to avoid deepening the justice gap.

pts.k: The source treats useful legal assistance as distinct from legal-exam performance and identifies harmful legal answers as a deployment risk.
pts.d: Hagan's research summaries argue that consumer legal Q&A needs task-specific, human-centered quality standards and that these standards can support system improvement and assessment of consumer harms. The incident-database project solicits examples of incorrect law, fabricated legal information, irrelevant answers and oversimplification; this is a risk taxonomy and collection effort, not a reported incidence or hallucination rate. A machine-translation post excerpt also cautions that general-context accuracy does not establish effectiveness in legal settings; the excerpt references lessons from Cristina Llop's work but does not provide a direct statement from her or quantitative results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists mainly of research methods, research outputs and prototype experience; the hub does not report aggregate gains in legal-service capacity or client outcomes.
pts.d: The Lab describes online and in-court interviews in which adults consider fictional legal problems and are observed using AI. It also describes expert interviews and a rating game using real user questions and model answers to build labeled datasets and refine quality criteria. Hagan's 2023 study proposes 22 criteria reviewed by legal-domain experts; her December 2024 paper reports a three-study sequence yielding a draft evaluation protocol. These support claims about developing standards and understanding user needs, rather than establishing that AI resolves more legal problems. The 2026 prototypes are described as functional and tested against real cases and feedback, but the hub gives no sample sizes, accuracy scores, control groups, quantified time savings or client-outcome estimates. LegalBench is separately summarized as an academic benchmark covering 162 tasks and six types of legal reasoning, with evaluation of 20 models; no model scores or access-to-justice effects are reproduced. Bibliographic listings alone are not treated as findings from the cited papers.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Benefits are predominantly conditional and prospective, with research and prototyping described across 2023–2026 rather than a fixed forecast for transformation.
pts.d: Although the supplied document heading labels the hub 2025, its content includes Winter–Spring 2026 course activity and a June 2026 workshop announcement. User research began at least by 2023 and is intended to continue as systems and public behavior change. The 2024–25 course scoped and developed pilots; Winter 2026 teams built prototypes, with Spring refinement and testing intended to prepare for possible pilots. The Lab conditions responsible use on legal accuracy, safety, privacy, human oversight, expert and user feedback, and attention to deployment processes and policies. Automated evaluation remains exploratory, not established as safe. There is no numerical forecast for closing the justice gap and no deadline for replacing professional services.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are underserved individuals and resource-constrained legal-help providers, with supporting roles for researchers, technologists, funders and regulators.
pts.d: Intended beneficiaries include tenants facing eviction or housing problems, unrepresented litigants, people navigating criminal-record relief or reentry-related financial obligations, and consumers seeking answers about civil legal problems. Non-English speakers are identified as potential beneficiaries of translation tools whose legal effectiveness remains uncertain. Legal aid attorneys, paralegals, junior attorneys, clinic volunteers and court staff are expected to gain workflow assistance rather than be displaced. Legal aid organizations, courts and technology partners are intended to benefit from reusable infrastructure, while researchers and regulators gain evaluation resources and funders gain visibility into projects. The context is unmet legal need and public protection, not enterprise legal-budget savings or predictions about law-firm staffing, billing or market share.
